name: Ahaziah (son of Ahab, king of Israel)
title: Son of Ahab, wicked king of Israel
summary: Ahaziah belonged to the Omride dynasty and ascended the throne of the northern kingdom after his father Ahab, but his reign from Samaria lasted only two years. Raised under the influence of Queen Jezebel and Baal worship's hold on the court, he continued his parents' religious apostasy. Politically, his rule was marked by decline: Moab broke away from Israelite dominance without Ahaziah being able to intervene. When he suffered a serious injury after falling through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria, he chose to send messengers to Baal-Zebub, the Philistine god of Ekron, to learn whether he would recover—a choice that revealed his deep distrust of Yahweh. The prophet Elijah intervened by God's command and met the messengers with an unyielding judgment: the king would never leave his sickbed. When Ahaziah sent soldiers to bring the prophet, the first two groups were consumed by fire from heaven, while the third was spared after their captain fell on his knees and pleaded for mercy. Elijah then delivered the judgment personally to the king. Ahaziah died without an heir, and the throne passed to his brother Joram—a dynastic shift that signaled the imminent downfall of the Omride house.

keyEvents.title: Ahaziah becomes king over Israel
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah became king over Israel in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat's reign and ruled for two years in Samaria.

keyEvents.title: Walked in his parents' evil ways
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah did what was evil in the Lord's sight, walking in the way of his father and mother, and in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin. He served Baal and worshiped him, provoking the anger of the Lord, the God of Israel.

keyEvents.title: Moab's Rebellion Against Israel
keyEvents.description: After Ahab's death, Moab rebelled against Israel. Ahaziah was unable to restore control over Moab during his short reign.

keyEvents.title: Ahaziah's Fall and Illness
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria and became seriously ill. He sent messengers to consult Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron, asking if he would recover.

keyEvents.title: Elijah's Judgment Against Ahaziah
keyEvents.description: The Lord's angel sent the prophet Elijah to meet Ahaziah's messengers with the message that the king would die because he sought Baal-Zebub instead of the God of Israel. The king sent three groups of fifty soldiers each to bring Elijah. Over the first two groups, Elijah called down fire from heaven. The leader of the third group fell on his knees and begged for their lives to be spared, and they were saved. Elijah went with them and delivered the judgment directly to the king.

keyEvents.title: Ahaziah's Death
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken. Since he had no son, his brother Joram became king in his place.

versions.summary: Ahaziah was the son of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, and he reigned over the northern kingdom of Israel for only two years. He followed in his parents' footsteps by worshiping Baal and doing what was evil in the Lord's sight. After falling through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria, he sent messengers to Baal-Zebub in Ekron seeking healing, but was met by the prophet Elijah who declared his death as punishment for his idolatry.
versions.title: The Wicked King of Israel
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Wicked King of Israel' is descriptive but could be made more precise by including that he was the son of Ahab, to distinguish him from the other Ahaziah (king of Judah). An alternative title could be 'Ahab's Son, Wicked King of Israel'.; [minor] Ahaziah was specifically 'king of Israel' (the Northern Kingdom). It may also be considered to add the role 'worshiper of Baal' to emphasize his religious character, but 'king' is the most important.; [minor] In the event 'Elijah's Judgment on Ahaziah', three groups of fifty soldiers were sent, not two. The third group humbled themselves, and their leader was spared (2 Kings 1:13–14). The description should be updated for accuracy.; [minor] Ahaziah's attempt to cooperate with Jehoshaphat in shipbuilding (mentioned in 2 Chronicles 20:35–37) could be included as a key event, but 1 Kings 22:49–50 attributes this initiative to Jehoshaphat. This may be considered an additional event.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. Notes should be added concerning Baal-zebub (linguistic/theological), the Moabite rebellion (historical/archaeological with reference to the Mesha Stele), and Ahaziah's short reign in the context of the Omride dynasty.; [minor] The life period 'c. 853–852 BC' indicates his reign, not his lifespan. It should be clarified that this is his reign, e.g., 'Reigned c. 853–852 BC'. His birth date is unknown.

versions.summary:
Ahaziah was the son of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, and he reigned over the northern kingdom of Israel for only two years.  
He followed in his parents' footsteps by worshiping Baal and doing what was evil in the Lord's sight.  
During his short reign, Moab rebelled against Israel.  
After falling through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria, he sent messengers to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, to ask whether he would recover – instead of seeking the God of Israel.  
The prophet Elijah was sent by the Lord to declare his death as punishment for this idolatry.  
Ahaziah died without leaving a son, and his brother Joram succeeded him on the throne.

Since an earlier version exists, the text should be rephrased to avoid reuse.; [minor] The description mentions that fire fell upon 'the first two groups', but the text could have been even clearer that the leader of the third group asked for mercy and was therefore spared (2 Kings 1:13-14). The source could possibly be changed to 'theological' unless a specific rabbinic tradition is added.; [minor] 1 Kings 22:52 mentions that Ahaziah became king, but verse 51 also provides context for the timing (Jehoshaphat's reign year). Consider including verse 51 for completeness.

versions.summary: As the second-to-last ruler of the Omride dynasty, Ahaziah ruled the northern kingdom of Israel for only two years from Samaria. Born into the house of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, he inherited not only the throne but also his parents' devotion to the Baal cult. His reign was marked by political instability: Moab broke free from Israeli overlordship, and Ahaziah failed to restore control. After falling through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria and being seriously injured, he sent messengers to Baal-zebub, the Philistine god of Ekron, to inquire about his fate—an act that revealed his fundamental distrust in Israel's God. The prophet Elijah confronted the king's envoys with a word of judgment: because Ahaziah had sought a foreign god instead of Yahweh, he would not rise from his sickbed. Ahaziah died childless, and his brother Joram succeeded him as king.
versions.title: Son of Ahab, wicked king of Israel
versions.reason: [minor] The role "last generation of the Omride dynasty" is more a description than a role. Ahaziah was the second-to-last king in the Omride dynasty (Joram came after him). Suggests changing to something more precise like "member of the Omride dynasty".; [minor] The summary describes Ahaziah as "the second-to-last ruler in the Omride dynasty", which is correct (Joram was the last). This is well phrased. But the sentence is very similar to the openings of the two previous versions. Suggests a slightly different opening to avoid repetition.; [minor] The description says "Fire fell from heaven over the first two groups" - technically it was Elijah who called down fire, not just passively that fire fell. Moreover, the text states that the leader of the third group "humbled himself" - in the original text he fell on his knees and pleaded for their lives to be spared, which is more precise than simply "humbled himself".

footnotes.text: The name Ahaziah (Hebrew: אֲחַזְיָה, ʾĂḥazyāh) means 'the Lord has grasped' or 'Yahweh holds fast.' It is ironic that a king with this theophoric name turned away from Yahweh to Baal-Zebub.

Baal-Zebub (בַּעַל זְבוּב) means 'lord of the flies' and was a Philistine god worshiped in Ekron. Many scholars believe the original name was Baal-Zebul ('the exalted lord'), and that Israelite authors deliberately distorted it into a derogatory form. In the New Testament, the form Beelzebul appears as a name for the prince of demons.

The Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone), discovered in 1868 in Dhiban, Jordan, confirms the biblical account of Moab's rebellion against Israel. The inscription from King Mesha of Moab describes how he freed Moab from Israeli domination after the time of the Omride dynasty, which corresponds with 2 Kings 1:1 and 3:4-5.

The Omride dynasty, to which Ahaziah belonged, is well documented in Assyrian sources. In Shalmaneser III's Black Obelisk and other inscriptions, Israel is referred to as 'Bit-Humri' (House of Omri) long after the dynasty had fallen, testifying to its historical significance.

Ahaziah's sending of messengers to Baal-Zebub in Ekron instead of seeking the God of Israel illustrates a recurring theme in the Books of Kings: kings' fates are determined by their faithfulness to Yahweh. Elijah's confrontation with Ahaziah's soldiers recalls his earlier confrontation with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and underscores Yahweh's sovereignty over life and death.

The event where three groups of fifty soldiers are sent to fetch Elijah testifies to the ongoing tension between royal power and prophetic movements in the Northern Kingdom. The fire from heaven that struck the first two groups is a theophanic motif with parallels to other narratives in the biblical tradition, including the destruction of Sodom and the events on Mount Carmel.

The fact that Ahaziah died childless and was succeeded by his brother Joram was unusual in the Israelite monarchy. Dynastic succession normally passed from father to son. The throne passing to a brother may indicate that Ahaziah's short and disastrous reign prevented him from establishing an heir, marking the beginning of the final fall of the Omride dynasty.
